passage:
Harsha, you think I was always this old man who cries at films? At fifteen I was told, 'Men don't cry, Yusuf.' When my elder brother left for work in the Gulf and I didn't know when I'd see him again, I went behind the well and bit my sleeve so no one would hear.
My Urdu teacher, Masterji, found me there. He didn't laugh. He sat down and said, 'Tears are not a woman's thing or a man's thing. They are a heart's thing.' Then he cried a little too, about his own son far away.
I have never forgotten that. So when your mother says you should keep quiet about becoming a pilot, I'll tell you what Masterji told me: the heart doesn't care about these rules. Say it out loud. I'll be the first to clap.

qa.q: Where did Yusuf go to cry when his brother left?
qa.a: Behind the well, biting his sleeve so no one would hear.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf hide his tears at fifteen?
qa.a: He had been told 'Men don't cry', so he felt sadness was not safe to show.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Yusuf saw crying?
qa.a: Masterji finding him, not laughing, saying tears are a heart's thing and then crying too, widened what felt allowed.

qa.q: What might Masterji have been feeling when he cried a little too?
qa.a: Masterji was probably missing his own son far away, and sitting with Yusuf let him share that sadness instead of hiding it.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a boy taught not to cry who hid his sadness, and adults who widen which feelings and ambitions feel safe.

passage:
Fifteen minutes before the annual day show, the stage lights failed, and everyone backstage was shouting. Gopika stood in a corner holding the host's script she had written herself. She'd wanted to host, but her aunt always said girls who push forward look proud, so she had let Arnav take it.
Farhan sat on a crate, jaw tight. His grandfather had gone into hospital that morning, and when his eyes filled at breakfast, his uncle had said, 'Be a man.'
Mrs Iyer, torch in hand, saw them both. To Farhan she said quietly, 'You're allowed to be worried. Sit with me a minute.' He let a few tears fall, and his shoulders dropped.
Then she handed Gopika the torch. 'Arnav's frozen. You know this script best. Will you open the show?'
Gopika hesitated, then stepped out.

qa.q: Why had Gopika let Arnav host?
qa.a: Her aunt always said girls who push forward look proud.

qa.q: What does Farhan's tight jaw suggest he was holding in?
qa.a: It suggests he was holding back worry and sadness about his grandfather after being told to 'be a man'.

qa.q: What choices did Mrs Iyer make that widened what felt safe for each teenager?
qa.a: She told Farhan he was allowed to be worried and sat with him, and she asked Gopika to open the show with the script she wrote.

qa.q: How might Arnav feel when Gopika steps out to open the show?
qa.a: Arnav, who had frozen, may feel relieved that someone who knows the script well has taken over.

grounding: Shows a boy hiding sadness and a girl hiding ambition because of learned gender rules, and an adult backstage who widens what feels safe for both.

passage: People think I'm shy. I'm Ishita, fifteen, and I'm not shy. I just learned early that girls in my family don't say, "I want to be a pilot." My aunts would laugh; my grandmother would say, "Be quiet, sit nicely." So I kept the aviation magazines under my mattress and said I wanted to be a teacher, which made everyone nod. Then last month my father, Ramesh, found one of the magazines. I was sure he'd be angry. Instead he sat on my bed and read it with me. He said, "Your grandmother had dreams too, you know. Nobody asked her." Then he said, "Say it out loud, Ishita. Here, where it's safe." So I did. "I want to be a pilot." It felt like breathing.

qa.q: Where did Ishita keep the aviation magazines?
qa.a: Under the mattress.

qa.q: How did Ishita feel when her father found the magazine?
qa.a: She was sure he would be angry and felt scared, then relieved and free when he read it with her.

qa.q: What did Ramesh do that widened what felt safe for Ishita?
qa.a: He read the magazine with her, spoke of her grandmother's unasked dreams and invited her to say her wish aloud.

qa.q: How might Ishita's grandmother have felt as a girl?
qa.a: She may have felt silenced, with dreams nobody ever asked about.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl hiding ambition because of gender rules, and a father who makes it safe to voice it.

passage:
Monday: When Pema's dog died, he wanted to cry, but his uncle said, "Boys don't cry, Pema. Be strong for your mother." So he kept his face still at school and in the courtyard.
Wednesday: He snapped at his friends and couldn't sleep. His mother, Minakshi, found him sitting alone by the empty kennel.
Friday: Minakshi sat beside him. "In this house anyone can cry. Your Papa cried when his father died. I saw." Pema's chin shook, and then the tears came, a long time's worth. Minakshi held him. Afterwards he said, "I miss him so much." "I know," she said. "Me too."

qa.q: Where did Minakshi find Pema?
qa.a: Sitting alone by the empty kennel.

qa.q: How was Pema feeling on Wednesday?
qa.a: He was sad and tense from holding in his grief, snapping at friends and unable to sleep.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do that widened what Pema could show?
qa.a: She told him anyone in the house can cry, shared that his Papa had cried, and held him.

qa.q: How might Pema's uncle see crying?
qa.a: His uncle sees it as weakness for boys and expects Pema to be strong instead.

grounding: Shows over days a teenage boy told not to cry who hides sadness, until a parent makes it safe to grieve.

passage: You asked why I started the dance club at our school, beta. Years ago I taught a boy called Joseph, fifteen, in Kochi. He danced beautifully, but only when he thought nobody was watching, behind the science block. When I asked him to join the annual day dance, he went red. "My father says dancing is for girls. I'm supposed to play football." So he played football, badly, looking miserable. I, Gargi, went to see his father. I didn't argue; I just showed him a video of Joseph dancing behind the science block. His father watched it twice. Then he said, quietly, "He looks happy." Joseph danced on annual day. His father sat in the front row.

qa.q: Where did Joseph dance when nobody was watching?
qa.a: Behind the science block.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when asked to join the annual day dance?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and torn, going red because his father saw dancing as only for girls.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Gargi showed Joseph's father the video instead of arguing, and he saw his son was happy.

qa.q: How did Joseph's father change?
qa.a: He moved from calling dance a girls' thing to seeing Joseph happy and sitting in the front row.

grounding: Shows a teenage boy hiding a love of dance because of gender rules, and an adult who helps widen what feels allowed.

passage:
The rain had flooded the road outside the school, and the buses were an hour late. Raghav and Ira waited in the empty staff room with Mrs Bose, the debate coach.
Raghav's grandfather had died on Sunday. When Mrs Bose asked how he was, Raghav said, "Fine, ma'am. Boys don't make a fuss." His jaw was clenched.
Ira had the form for school captain folded in her bag. She hadn't filled it in. "My aunt says girls who push too much look proud," she mumbled.
Mrs Bose put down her tea. "In this room, crying is allowed, Raghav. And Ira, wanting to lead isn't pride."
Raghav's eyes filled, and for once he didn't wipe them away. Ira pulled out the form. By the time the bus horn sounded through the rain, her name was on it.

qa.q: Why were Raghav and Ira waiting in the staff room?
qa.a: The rain had flooded the road outside the school, and the buses were an hour late.

qa.q: What did Raghav's clenched jaw suggest about how he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggested he was holding back deep sadness about his grandfather because he believed boys shouldn't make a fuss.

qa.q: What did Mrs Bose do that could help other teenagers?
qa.a: She gave clear permission for both a boy's tears and a girl's ambition, widening what each of them felt safe to show.

qa.q: How might Ira see Raghav crying in front of her?
qa.a: She may feel moved and trusted, and it might make her braver about showing her own hidden wish to lead.

grounding: Raghav hides sadness and Ira hides ambition because of learned gender rules, until an adult widens the range of what they may show.
